newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr rally stalls well short of safety.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr rally stalls well short of safety.

text.p: The Australian dollar settled into nervous consolidation at the midsession after a short covering bounce stopped well short of safe territory.

Dealers said sentiment remained bleak amid expectations of another cut in domestic rates and on-going weakness in commodity prices, so the interbank market was looking to sell into rallies, as had already been seen at US$0.7470.

But the market was already very short of dollars which made it reluctant to test bids beneath US$0.7420, at least for the moment. Many reckoned the 1/2 cent range would hold until June jobs data on Thursday updated the outlook for monetary policy.
By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the dollar was idling at US$0.7455/60 having edged back from an early US$0.7470 and a US$0.7493 high overnight, but was still up on Tuesday's late US$0.7418/23.
The latter was the currency's lowest close since January last year and came after Prime Minister John Howard singalled the government's desire to see lower interest rates.

Analysts reckon that wether the RBA obliges depends mostly on what Q2 consumer price and wages data have to say about inflation when they are released on July 23/24. Most felt tomorrow's employment figures would only be significant in the policy equation if the outcome was way outside forecasts.
Median estimates favour a rise of around 40,250 in employment for June, almost exactly correcting the shock 40,300 fall recorded in May.

The unemployment rate was seen edging down to 8.7 percent from 8.8 percent, although analysts cautioned that this depended largely on the volatile participation rate not recovering all of the sharp fall suffered in May.

It would take an increase of more than 60,000 for the trend in employment growth to pick up even slightly and many suspected a jaded market would not be impressed by anything less than a 100,000 new jobs, an outcome not unknown in the past.
A firm result was likely to prompt knee-jerk short covering and perhaps lift the dollar above 75 cents, although stiff resistance was expected at US$0.7530 and US$0.7550.

Equally, anything less than a 30,000 gain would be considered weak and an actual fall in employment would have the money market baying for an immediate cut in official rates and could see the dollar testing US$0.7410 again.

On the crosses the local currency lost early gains against the yen, to stand at 83.90/00 from 84.20/30, in the wake of figures showing Japan's current account surplus surged 155 percent in May to 906.8 billion yen.
The result was pretty much as the market expected but no less negative for that as it promised to keep trade tensions rumbling between Japan and the U.S.
The trade data also implied a net flow into the yen equal to the surplus, or in this case over 900 billion yen, which would tend to support the currency.

However, analysts noted that in the same period Japanese investors bought a total of 2.53 trillion yen of foreign bonds and stocks while offshore investors bought a net 941 billion yen of Japanese equity and debt.
That implied a net need by the Japanese to buy 1.59 trillion yen of foreign currency, quite a bit more than the demand for yen implied by the trade surplus.
This would normally act to restrain the yen but the market's political concerns were dominating at the moment and the U.S. dollar slipped to 112.57/62 yen after the data from an early 113.10/15.
In trade weighted terms it was up at 56.7 from Tuesday's weak 56.5 close, but down on the opening 57.0.
